justification: The only provided article (PMID 41293172) is a bioinformatic prognostic signature for colorectal cancer that lists HDHD5 among mitochondrial lipid metabolism-related genes; it contains no measurement of alkaline phosphatase and no human genetic variant analysis relating HDHD5 to alkaline phosphatase levels. There are no GWAS, family, or cohort studies in this list linking HDHD5 variants to serum alkaline phosphatase, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported. A small amount of weight is given to Hypothesized because HDHD5 (CECR5) belongs to the haloacid dehalogenase-like hydrolase/phosphatase superfamily, giving a faint biological rationale for a phosphatase-related phenotype, but this is not demonstrated in the provided literature. The co-mention is essentially incidental, so Novel receives the bulk of the probability.

None of the provided articles mention high density lipoprotein, lipid metabolism, or any cardiometabolic trait in connection with KNL1/CASC5. The literature exclusively concerns kinetochore assembly, spindle assembly checkpoint signaling, autosomal recessive primary microcephaly (MCPH4), cancer genomics, and evolutionary genetics. The only cardiac-related paper (PMID 37905452) involves Knl1 downstream of ATF4 in mouse cardiomyocyte proliferation, which is unrelated to HDL cholesterol levels. There is no human genetic or biological evidence linking KNL1 variation to HDL, so the relationship is best classified as Novel.

None of the provided articles examine body mass index or any adiposity/obesity-related phenotype in relation to MIB1. The literature set concerns MIB1/Mib2 as Notch-ligand E3 ubiquitin ligases in cardiac trabeculation and left ventricular noncompaction, neurogenesis, cilia regulation, synaptic glutamate receptor localization, aortic aneurysm modeling, and DNA repair/chemoresistance. The closest tangential biology is Mib1 involvement in pancreatic endocrine progenitor development in mice (PMID 30093553), which could weakly support a metabolic hypothesis, but there are no human genetic variant studies linking MIB1 to BMI. No human probands, families, or cohorts with BMI associations are reported, precluding Existing or Established.

None of the provided articles report human genetic variants in MIB1 associated with Type 2 diabetes or any glycemic trait, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. The only biologically relevant evidence is the mouse study (PMID 30093553) showing that Mib1 mutants have near-total depletion of dorsal pancreatic progenitors with an anterior Gcg+ endocrine extension, implicating Mib1 in Notch-dependent pancreatic endocrine/islet development—a plausible mechanistic link to diabetes, but only in animal models. The remaining papers concern cardiac trabeculation, aortic aneurysm, zebrafish neurogenesis, Drosophila glutamate receptors, MIB2-related gastropathy/LVNC, and miRNA networks in cerebral cavernous malformations, all irrelevant to Type 2 diabetes. Thus the evidence supports at most a hypothesized relationship based on developmental biology of the endocrine pancreas, with a substantial chance that the association is incidental/novel.

phenotype: Eosinophils/100 leukocytes in Blood by Automated count
justification: Two independent human genetic studies report direct results linking ALOX15 variants to blood eosinophil counts: the UK Biobank gene-based whole-exome analysis of eosinophil count found ALOX15 among genes driven by rare variants independent of GWAS common variants (PMID 35935937), and a Korean cohort study showed that ALOX15 promoter genotypes/haplotypes (-427G/A, haplotype GCG) were associated with significantly higher peripheral total eosinophil counts, with supporting promoter reporter assays (PMID 22652554). Additional human genetic support comes from the Icelandic/UK GWAS where the ALOX15 loss-of-function p.Thr560Met variant confers protection against nasal polyps/chronic rhinosinusitis, a strongly eosinophil-linked trait, with eosinophil-count markers explicitly examined (PMID 30643255). Extensive expression and functional data (eosinophilic CRS, EoE, benralizumab eosinophil-depletion transcriptomics) corroborate ALOX15 as an eosinophil-associated gene, reinforcing biological plausibility. The main residual uncertainty is whether the exact phenotype "eosinophil percentage by automated count" is directly replicated, which keeps meaningful weight on Existing.

phenotype: Eosinophils [#/volume] in Blood by Automated count
justification: The strongest direct evidence is the UK Biobank whole-exome gene-based analysis (PMID 35935937), which explicitly reports ALOX15 among genes whose rare variants are associated with eosinophil count independent of known common GWAS signals — a large human cohort result. The deCODE/UK Biobank study (PMID 30643255) identifies the ALOX15 p.Thr560Met loss-of-function variant in nasal polyps/chronic rhinosinusitis and frames it within eosinophil-count-associated markers, but its own results concern polyps rather than eosinophil counts, so it serves as supporting/precursor-phenotype evidence rather than independent replication of the count trait. Additional human work links ALOX15 variants to eosinophilic airway disease (PMIDs 26067486, 34486255, 36470944), and benralizumab transcriptomics (PMID 30658649) shows ALOX15 expression tracks eosinophil depletion, reinforcing biological plausibility. Because only one cited study directly demonstrates the variant–eosinophil count association in its own results, I weight Existing above Established, while retaining substantial probability for Established given the size and quality of that cohort analysis.

Multiple independent human studies report FLNA variants in probands with macrothrombocytopenia and platelet functional defects: PMID 23117662 describes four unrelated patients with distinct FLNA mutations, platelet FLNa deficiency, thrombocytopenia and altered aggregation/adhesion; PMID 21960593 reports three patients with FLNA mutations and abnormal megakaryopoiesis/macrothrombocytopenia; PMID 29449050 documents a de novo FLNA nonsense variant with chronic thrombocytopenia and FLNa-negative platelets; PMID 28428218 characterizes a male patient with a C-terminal FLNA extension causing gain-of-function platelet integrin αIIbβ3 activation; PMID 26133172 and PMID 35156755 add further independent patients with platelet phenotypes. These are original human genetic/functional results in separate probands, supported by mechanistic mouse and iPSC work (PMIDs 21652675, 36006037, 30602618) and a dedicated variant-curation paper (PMID 32299270). The evidence is replicated and causal, so the relationship is Established.

None of the provided articles examine body weight or any weight-related anthropometric trait in relation to KIF1B. The literature clusters into three unrelated topics: pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma susceptibility (PMIDs 24899893, 33362715, 23061808, 33397043), inherited peripheral neuropathies/CMT2A (PMIDs 11389829, 32298515, 25802885), and HBV-related hepatocellular carcinoma/multiple sclerosis GWAS loci (PMIDs 26255971, 22363396, 18997785). The only tangentially relevant observation is that KIF1B heterozygous mice and CMT2A patients show progressive muscle weakness and axonal transport defects (PMID 11389829) — muscle weakness/wasting is not body weight, and this is a murine/neuropathy phenotype rather than a weight measurement. No human study reports KIF1B variants associated with weight, BMI, obesity, or growth, so the association is essentially unsupported; a small allowance is kept for indirect biological plausibility via neuromuscular wasting or catecholamine-secreting tumors (which can cause weight loss).

None of the provided articles examine anthropometric traits such as hip circumference, body fat distribution, adiposity, or any related metabolic/body-size phenotype. The KIF1B literature here concerns Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A and axonal transport, lysosome trafficking, neuroblastoma, pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma susceptibility, multiple sclerosis, erythromelalgia, and HBV-related hepatocellular carcinoma (rs17401966). No genetic association study, family study, or functional work links KIF1B variation or biology to hip circumference, and no plausible mechanistic pathway to body size/fat distribution is suggested. The co-mentions are incidental, so the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a small allowance for indirect biological speculation.

Human genetic evidence linking the α-globin locus to MCHC exists: the eMERGE GWAS in African-Americans (PMID 23696099) found rs9924561 at HBA1/HBA2 associated with MCV, MCH and MCHC with discovery and replication cohorts, and the African HbA1c PheWAS (PMID 40446072) reports variants associated with MCHC attributed to α-thalassaemia (HBA1/HBA2) deletions. Clinical cohorts likewise show significantly reduced MCHC in carriers of α-thalassaemia alleles (PMIDs 2420505, 15919031, 39991167). However, most of this evidence is at the level of the α-globin cluster or of multi-gene -α3.7 deletions, which cannot isolate HBA2 from HBA1; the studies reporting specific HBA2 point mutations (Hb Westmead, Hb Constant Spring, Hb Adana; PMIDs 32436451, 32338097, 27271331) focus on Hb, MCV and MCH rather than MCHC. Therefore the association is well supported at the locus level but only indirectly attributable to HBA2 itself, leaving Established and Existing nearly balanced.

None of the provided articles examine anthropometric height or stature; all concern MICA as an MHC class I chain-related immune gene in contexts such as Takayasu arteritis, Behçet disease, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, hepatocellular carcinoma, transplantation, type 1 diabetes, gout, and cervical cancer. No study reports variants in MICA associated with height, nor any biological pathway (growth plate, GH/IGF axis, skeletal development) that would plausibly link MICA to stature. The gene's described function—NKG2D ligand mediating NK and T-cell cytotoxicity—provides no mechanistic basis for height regulation. Co-mentions, if any, would be incidental, so the evidence supports a Novel classification with only a small allowance for unexamined pleiotropy within the highly polymorphic MHC region.

No articles were provided, so there is no literature evidence linking GOLGA6C variants or biology to height. GOLGA6C is a golgin family member located in a segmentally duplicated, highly polymorphic region (chromosome 15q), and such genes are frequently poorly covered by GWAS arrays and sequencing, making well-documented associations unlikely. Without any cited human genetic studies, functional data, or animal models, the relationship cannot be classified beyond Novel. A small residual probability is retained for the possibility of uncited GWAS catalog entries or biological plausibility arguments.

phenotype: Erythrocytes [#/volume] in Blood by Automated count
justification: No human study in this set reports variants in CBFA2T3 associated with automated erythrocyte count; the human literature is dominated by somatic CBFA2T3::GLIS2 fusions in pediatric acute megakaryoblastic/myeloid leukemia (PMIDs 23153540, 23407549, 31719049, 28063190) and unrelated phenotypes (CSF Aβ42 decline, PMID 31370031; splenic marginal zone lymphoma somatic mutations, PMID 24349473). The strongest phenotype-relevant evidence is a GWAS in the blood clam Anadara granosa where a Cbfa2t3 3'UTR SNP associated with red blood traits and promoted blood cell proliferation (PMID 39367301) — compelling biology but non-human, so it supports Hypothesized rather than Existing. CBFA2T3 (MTG16/ETO2) is an established hematopoietic transcriptional corepressor central to erythro-megakaryocytic lineage programs, giving a clear biological rationale for influencing erythrocyte counts without direct human genetic association evidence here. A small residual probability is retained for Novel (purely incidental co-mention) and Existing (possible unreported human blood-trait GWAS signal).

Multiple independent human studies report EMD (emerin/STA) point mutations in probands and families with atrial arrhythmias including atrial fibrillation/flutter: PMID 18266676 maps a Lys37del EMD deletion to X-linked nonsyndromic sinus node dysfunction and AF in a multigenerational family; PMID 15967842 describes a nonsense EMD mutation in two EDMD families with AF in carriers and sudden death; PMID 11063761 reports a novel 417insT EMD mutation in a four-generation family with episodes of atrial fibrillation; PMID 25502304 reports AF with the c.449+1G>A emerin splice-site mutation; and PMID 33673224 is a genotype-stratified cohort showing AF/AFl in 50% of EMD-mutated patients. These are independent probands/families with single-gene (non-CNV) variants, satisfying replication criteria. Additional reviews (PMIDs 35453731, 36813137, 30130999) restate the association as background and only reinforce, rather than establish, the link. Residual probability is left for "Existing" in case one considers much of the EMD-AF evidence to arise within the broader EDMD syndrome rather than as isolated AF causation.

None of the supplied articles report a genetic association between STK38 variants and mean platelet volume. The only paper mentioning MPV (PMID 37626602) is a clinical inflammatory-biomarker study in diabetic retinopathy with no genetic or STK38 content, making it an incidental co-mention. The STK38/NDR1 literature here concerns Hippo-pathway signaling, autophagy, nuclear export, DNA repair, hepatic lipid metabolism, and GWAS/TWAS for unrelated phenotypes (cocaine dependence, rheumatoid arthritis, congenital solitary functioning kidney, cardiomyopathy), none of which address platelet size or megakaryocyte biology. At most, a weak hypothetical basis could be argued from STK38's broad roles in cell proliferation, cytoskeletal/Hippo signaling and inflammation, which could plausibly touch megakaryopoiesis, but no direct evidence is presented. Therefore the evidence base in this set supports "Novel" with some residual probability for "Hypothesized".

Multiple independent human studies report ABCB4 variants directly associated with elevated serum gamma-glutamyltransferase. PMID 36397154 genotyped the ABCB4 c.711A>T variant in two independent Polish PBC/PSC cohorts (867 patients) and found the risk allele associated with increased serum GGT, ALP and AST. PMID 33554096 (308 LPAC cases vs 206 controls) found ABCB4 variants associated with chronic GGT elevation, and PMID 21119540 molecularly characterized 133 children with high-γ-GT intrahepatic cholestasis, identifying ABCB4 mutations in 28 probands with genotype–phenotype correlation. Additional cohorts and probands (PMIDs 17726488, 26324191, 22766396, 37511794) replicate the high-GGT cholestatic phenotype of ABCB4 (MDR3) deficiency in humans, in contrast to low-GGT PFIC1/2. The evidence is therefore replicated, human, and variant-level, supporting an Established relationship, with a small residual allowance that "GGT level" as a quantitative trait is partly reported as a disease feature rather than a primary association endpoint.

The only direct genetic evidence is the exome-chip meta-analysis of blood cell traits (PMID 27399967), which reports IL17RA among new loci for monocyte count in large multi-ancestry human cohorts with replication; this is a single primary study rather than multiple independent reports, so "Established" cannot be firmly claimed. Supporting mechanistic plausibility comes from PMID 23220496, where IL17RA promoter SNPs altered IL17RA protein/mRNA expression specifically in human CD14+ peripheral blood monocytes, linking common variation to monocyte biology. Other listed articles concern IL-17RA deficiency and candidiasis, psoriasis, ankylosing spondylitis, or NAFLD (PMIDs 27930337, 40571687, 27415816, 31311600), which are not monocyte-percentage phenotypes, and the CNV study (PMID 24692264) spans multiple genes and cannot isolate IL17RA. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with meaningful residual probability for "Established" given the strength and size of the exome-chip study.

All articles explicitly about "APC" and gastric ulceration (PMIDs 19409889, 17659730, 23523691, and the LPA/diet study 28050783 which only mentions ulceration in passing) use APC as the acronym for allylpyrocatechol, a Piper betel phenol, not the adenomatous polyposis coli gene; these are homonym papers and must be dismissed. The genuine APC gene literature concerns familial adenomatous polyposis, colorectal adenoma–carcinoma progression, β-catenin regulation, and mouse/Xenopus models (PMIDs 11516998, 8111410, 25243319, 31810128, 26097888), with gastric involvement limited to fundic gland/gastric polyps and, in Apc(Min/+) mice, gastritis, atrophy, intestinal metaplasia and dysplasia — not peptic/gastric ulcer. No human study here reports APC variants in gastric ulcer probands or families, so Established and Existing are essentially excluded. A modest Hypothesized weight is justified by the mouse gastric mucosal injury/inflammation phenotype (PMID 31810128) and human FAP gastric polyposis, which provide only indirect biological plausibility for gastric mucosal pathology.

Multiple independent human studies report IGF1R sequence variants associated with weight phenotypes in their own results. PMID 39809772 is a large whole-exome rare-variant burden analysis (up to 234,675 participants) identifying IGF1R as a determinant of birth weight with fetal and maternal effects, replicated in an independent sample. PMID 31586944 describes 35 patients with IGF1R point variants (not only deletions), overwhelmingly born small for gestational age with reduced birth weight, and PMID 21811077 reports a four-member Italian pedigree with a novel p.Tyr387X variant and birth weight SDS of -1.65 to -2.37. Additional support comes from a candidate-gene cohort where IGF1R rs4966035 associated with birth length and weight (PMID 24280783), a genome-wide linkage of an IGF1R CA repeat to fat-free mass (PMID 10690945), and an interventional cohort where IGF1R genotype modified weight change (PMID 15127203). These constitute replicated, human, variant-level evidence, supporting the Established category, with residual probability assigned to Existing since some phenotypes are growth/birth-size rather than adult body weight.

Multiple independent human genetic studies report their own results linking LMX1B variants to body weight/BMI: a large GWAS meta-analysis of childhood BMI (PMID 26604143, ~35,668 discovery + 11,873 replication children) found the LMX1B locus at genome-wide significance; an independent Mexican pediatric cohort replicated LMX1B/rs3829849 association with BMI and obesity (PMID 31936053); a Chinese cohort found rs10733682 associated with overweight/obesity in girls (PMID 32357537); and the LOGIC intervention cohort found rs10733682 associated with magnitude of body weight reduction (PMID 33315090). These are single-SNP associations in multiple independent human cohorts and ancestries, not copy-number events or mere background citations. Additional human studies examine the same variant in relation to satiety responsiveness and intrauterine diabetes interaction (PMIDs 28245097, 34205853), supporting consistency. The large remaining literature concerns nail-patella syndrome/nephropathy, which is unrelated to weight, so it neither strengthens nor weakens the weight association.

The strongest human evidence is the population-scale whole-genome sequencing study (PMID 41073786), which reports that protein-truncating variants in IRS2 are associated with chronic kidney disease independent of diabetes status in UK Biobank and All of Us — CKD being defined largely by creatinine-based eGFR, a well-recognized direct correlate of serum creatinine. Additional human genetic support is indirect: reviews cite replication of the MYO16/IRS2 locus in diabetic nephropathy GWAS (PMIDs 26069720, 34609116), but these are secondary restatements rather than primary results, so they cannot establish replication. Supporting biology comes from non-human work: IRS2-knockout mice show albuminuria and altered renal hemodynamics with serum creatinine measured (PMID 33270683), and IRS2-dependent proximal tubule sodium transport (PMID 28428931), which would support only "Hypothesized" on their own. Because only one primary human study directly demonstrates a variant-level kidney-function association, "Existing" is the most appropriate category, with limited probability for "Established".

The UK Biobank exome sequencing study (PMID 33087929) reports in its own results that predicted loss-of-function variants in GMPR have large effects on blood cell traits, which plausibly includes hemoglobin/erythrocyte measures — this is credible human variant-level evidence, but it is a single cohort and the specific trait (hemoglobin concentration) is not explicitly named. No second independent human cohort, family, or proband series in this list replicates a GMPR–hemoglobin association; the 6p22.3 deletion case (PMID 23324214) spans multiple genes (ATXN1, DTNBP1, JARID2, MYLIP, GMPR) and cannot isolate GMPR, and the lipid GWAS hits at MYLIP/GMPR (PMIDs 19936222, 20864672) concern lipoproteins, not hemoglobin. Supporting biological plausibility comes from human whole-blood transcriptomics showing GMPR among erythropoiesis-responsive genes during microdose rHuEpo administration (PMID 29143667) and GMPR's role in purine/porphyrin-linked metabolism (PMIDs 41758903, 26853689), which supports a Hypothesized floor. Therefore Existing is the most probable category, with some weight for Established given the strong exome-wide blood-cell-trait finding.

All retrieved articles concern CKAP5/ch-TOG/XMAP215 as a microtubule polymerase involved in spindle assembly, ciliogenesis, oocyte meiotic maturation, and tumor cytoskeletal biology; none address waist-hip ratio (WHR), adiposity, body fat distribution, or any anthropometric/metabolic trait. There are no GWAS, family, or cohort studies linking CKAP5 variants to WHR, and no animal or expression data connecting it to adipose tissue distribution. The human genetic findings reported (TUBB8, KIF11, CKAP5 variants) relate to IVF failure and oocyte maturation arrest, which is unrelated to WHR. Any co-mention of "WHR" would be incidental, and the biology provides no plausible mechanistic bridge to fat distribution, so the relationship is best classified as Novel.

The strongest direct evidence is the ExomeChip/large-cohort analysis of rare and low-frequency coding variants altering human adult height (PMID 28146470), which explicitly highlights ADAMTS3 as a newly implicated biological candidate for growth; this is a single (albeit very large, human) study and therefore satisfies "Existing" but not replicated "Established". The familial 4q13.3 microdeletion with short stature (PMID 32299451) involves a multigene CNV (ADAMTS3, ANKRD17, COX18, GC, NPFFR2) and cannot single out ADAMTS3, so it does not count as independent confirmation. Other ADAMTS3 human variant reports concern Hennekam lymphangiectasia-lymphedema syndrome (PMIDs 28985353, 30450763, 37583869), which is a lymphatic dysplasia rather than a height phenotype, and the sheep splice variant (PMID 39409761) is non-human. Supportive biology exists (ADAMTS3 as a procollagen N-proteinase/ECM enzyme, growth-trait GWAS in goats, PMIDs 29885460, 41687347), which backs a hypothesized mechanism, but the human height association itself is best described as Existing with some chance of Established given the size/robustness of the height consortium data.

Multiple independent human studies report PCSK1 variants associated with body weight/BMI/obesity: a GWAS meta-analysis in >80,000 East Asians identified PCSK1 as a genome-wide significant BMI locus (PMID 22344219); a HuGE systematic review/meta-analysis confirmed rs6232/rs6234-rs6235 associations with obesity and BMI (PMID 25355447); a novel nonsense PCSK1 variant co-segregated with obesity in a three-generation French family with functional validation (PMID 24890885); rs6232 was associated with childhood and class III obesity in Mexicans (PMID 22737226); common haplotypes were associated with obesity in Chinese (PMID 19875984); and additional family-based Thai and multi-ethnic American cohorts report associations (PMIDs 24964673, 23451278). Rare-variant burden analyses also link PCSK1 to population-level BMI (PMID 39910307), and monogenic obesity cohorts include biallelic PCSK1 cases with characteristic BMI trajectories (PMID 40246357). Evidence is human, replicated across independent probands, families and cohorts, supporting "Established".

The only article directly linking IRS2 to acute renal failure is a mouse study (PMID 16306169) showing that ghrelin's protective effect against ischemia/reperfusion-induced acute renal failure is abolished in insulin receptor substrate-2 knockout mice, implicating IRS2 biology in renal ischemic injury — animal/functional evidence only, not human genetic variants. Additional supporting biology comes from IRS2-dependent insulin signaling in renal proximal tubule sodium transport (PMID 28428931), which is relevant to kidney function but not to acute kidney failure variants. All other papers concern IRS2 in insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, beta-cell function, longevity, PCOS, or diabetic nephropathy, with no human association studies for acute kidney injury. No human probands or families with IRS2 variants causing acute kidney failure are reported, so Established and Existing are not supportable. The weight therefore falls overwhelmingly on Hypothesized.

Only one article in this list reports alkaline phosphatase (ALP) as a direct outcome: PMID 34216018, which performed a GWAS of ALT, AST, ALP and bilirubin in 312,671 UK Biobank participants and found GPAM rs10787429 strongly associated with ALP (P = 9.5 × 10⁻³⁰), with replication in an independent Mass General Brigham cohort. This is credible human genetic evidence with internal replication, but it stems from a single publication, so the "two independent papers demonstrating the link in their own results" threshold for Established is not met. The remaining papers (e.g., PMIDs 33347879, 38632349, 34957434, 36280732) provide robust human evidence linking GPAM variants to closely related liver biochemistry and disease traits (ALT, AST, hepatic steatosis, cirrhosis), which supports ALP as part of the same liver-injury phenotype but does not independently measure ALP. Therefore the evidence best fits Existing, with meaningful probability for Established given the large, replicated ALP-specific signal.

Only one article in this set mentions platelets at all: a single case report of an adult with ADPKD-associated congenital hepatic fibrosis carrying compound heterozygous PKD1 variants (c.8296T>C, c.9653G>C) who had splenomegaly and a reduced platelet count (PMID 38384417). This thrombocytopenia is a secondary consequence of portal hypertension/hypersplenism rather than a direct PKD1 effect on platelet biology, and it is a single unreplicated proband, so "Established" is untenable. All other papers are PKD1/PKD2 mutation-screening and ADPKD molecular-diagnostic studies with no platelet phenotype whatsoever, making them incidental co-mentions. The evidence therefore sits between "Novel" (platelets essentially unaddressed) and "Existing" (one human case in which a PKD1-driven phenotype included low platelets), with limited mechanistic/biological rationale supporting "Hypothesized".

Nearly all of the provided articles are oncology drug trials (PARP inhibitors, platinum, taxanes, lurbinectedin) in which leukopenia/neutropenia appears as a treatment-emergent toxicity in cohorts selected for BRCA1/2 mutations; these report drug effects, not an effect of BRCA1 variants on white blood cell count, so they cannot establish the gene–phenotype link. The one study that directly tests germline BRCA status against hematologic toxicity is PMID 32497289, which found leukopenia and anemia to be significantly more frequent in BRCA non-carriers, with BRCA2 status an independent predictor of decreased hematologic toxicity—a human genotype–phenotype observation, though of inverse direction and driven more by BRCA2 than BRCA1. There is biologic plausibility, since BRCA1 loss impairs DNA damage repair in rapidly dividing hematopoietic progenitors and BRCA-deficient patients receive DNA-damaging agents that cause marked myelosuppression, which supports the Hypothesized tier. No two independent human studies with BRCA1 variants directly associated with decreased WBC count are present, so Established is not supportable. Points are therefore concentrated in Existing and Hypothesized, with a meaningful residual for Novel given the largely incidental co-mention pattern.

The only direct genetic evidence linking COL18A1 to HDL cholesterol comes from a single exome-array study (PMID 24507774), which reported the low-frequency coding variant rs114139997 (p.Gly111Arg) with a large effect on HDL-C and/or triglycerides in ~56,000 European- and African-ancestry individuals. Although this is a large, well-powered human study, it is a single publication, and I cannot cite a second independent human report replicating the COL18A1–HDL association, so "Established" cannot be awarded. Supporting but indirect human evidence includes COL18A1 expression during human adipocyte differentiation and an association of the c.1136C>T frizzled-motif variant with obesity in type 2 diabetes patients, with lipid covariates considered (PMID 18345385), which is a lipid-related metabolic phenotype rather than HDL itself. The remaining articles concern Knobloch syndrome, blood pressure/endothelial genes, tumors, or Drosophila, and do not bear on HDL. Hence "Existing" is the most probable category, with some residual probability for "Established" given the size and multi-cohort nature of the single discovery study.

Multiple independent human studies report their own results linking EGLN1 variants to hemoglobin concentration: Simonson et al. found positively selected EGLN1 haplotypes significantly associated with decreased hemoglobin in Tibetans (PMID 20466884); Lorenzo/Xiang et al. identified the Tibetan-specific EGLN1 D4E (rs186996510) variant significantly associated with hemoglobin levels (PMID 23666208); and an independent Andean highlander cohort in Bolivia showed EGLN1 haplotype frequencies correlated with Hb concentration (PMID 33282944). Additionally, germline loss-of-function EGLN1/PHD2 mutations cause familial erythrocytosis with elevated hemoglobin in multiple probands and families (PMIDs 24482100, 40627222, 27774468, 29790589). These represent replicated associations across distinct populations, ancestries, and clinical presentations, with both low-Hb adaptive variants and high-Hb pathogenic variants. The evidence is therefore clearly Established in humans.

PKD2 variants are a confirmed cause of ADPKD (PMIDs 40126492, 36573973, 24611717), and hypertension/elevated systolic blood pressure is a core, early, and well-recognized feature of ADPKD, making it a disease mechanism strongly linked to higher mean systolic BP. One human cohort directly measured systolic BP in ADPKD patients carrying truncating PKD1 or PKD2 mutations and found significantly higher SBP than controls (PMID 38892431), and a clinical review documents higher SBP/DBP in ADPKD including PKD2-mutated patients (PMID 38096797). However, these studies pool PKD1 and PKD2 carriers and do not isolate a PKD2-specific, replicated quantitative association with systolic BP, so the direct gene-specific evidence falls short of "Established." Supporting mechanistic data (TRPP2/polycystin-2 upregulation in VSMCs of salt-hypertensive rats, PMID 25351462; Pkd1+/- mouse aorta with altered Pkd2 expression and raised SBP, PMID 18679710) are animal/in vitro and therefore count toward Hypothesized rather than human evidence.

One human GWAS in the provided set (PMID 28158719, HCHS/SOL Hispanic/Latino cohort) directly reports a novel association of the CEBPE-SLC7A7 locus with basophil count, with the minor allele linked to lower basophil levels — this is direct, human, variant-level evidence for the gene–trait relationship. However, no second independent cohort or family study in this list replicates the CEBPE–basophil association; the remaining CEBPE papers concern childhood ALL susceptibility (rs2239633/rs2239630), specific granule deficiency, or longevity, and only support plausible myeloid-lineage biology rather than the basophil trait itself. The SGD and C/EBPε functional papers (PMIDs 11753076, 26019275, 35726044) document that loss of C/EBPε disrupts granulocyte granule gene expression and eosinophil/neutrophil maturation in humans, which strengthens biological plausibility and mechanistic linkage to granulocyte subset counts. Because the direct genetic evidence rests essentially on a single (albeit large and credible) association study, "Existing" is the best fit, with some probability retained for "Established" given the locus's recurrence in blood-cell trait literature.

phenotype: Eosinophils/100 leukocytes in Blood by Automated count
justification: The great majority of the retrieved articles concern protein "C2 domains" (calpain-5, Munc13-4, PKCalpha, ferlins, PI3K, PTEN, Nedd4-2, Notch ligands), which are homonymous usages and not the complement C2 gene; the asthma/theophylline paper uses "C2" merely as a treatment-group label. The genuine complement C2 papers address classical-pathway bypass, siRNA therapy of murine myasthenia gravis, CRIT receptor endocytosis, and a human SLE association (rs2844455), none of which examine eosinophil counts or any closely related hematological trait. No human genetic study here reports C2 variants associated with automated eosinophil percentage, so Established and Existing are not supportable. Some residual weight to Hypothesized is given because complement activation products (C3a/C5a derived downstream of C2-containing C3 convertase) can modulate eosinophil recruitment in allergic inflammation, providing a plausible but indirect biological rationale.

None of the provided articles report any human genetic variant in SCARF1 associated with mean platelet volume or any platelet trait, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported. The literature instead focuses on SCARF1 as an efferocytosis/scavenger receptor in autoimmunity (PMIDs 23892722, 35082161, 41673107), endothelial biology and adhesion (PMIDs 29242513, 11978792, 12154095), and TB transcriptomic signatures (PMIDs 30919880, 32517725). Weak indirect biological plausibility arises from SCARF1 expression in vascular endothelium and hematopoietic/endothelial precursor development in zebrafish cloche mutants (PMID 15802528) and from its requirement for C1q-driven NETosis that modulates coagulation (PMID 40997304), which could tangentially relate to platelet/megakaryocyte biology. However, these are not platelet-volume relevant findings, so the relationship is best described as novel, with a modest allowance for hypothesized based on vascular/coagulation biology.

No study in this list directly measures hip circumference, but multiple human genetic studies link rare protein-truncating variants in BSN to adiposity traits: exome-sequence analysis of up to 587,027 individuals found large BMI effects for BSN PTVs (PMID 38575728), this was replicated in the diverse All of Us cohort (PMID 39228706), and population-level BMI association of rare deleterious BSN variants was reported alongside the human hypothalamus atlas (PMID 39910307). BSN PTV carriers also show obesity in neurodevelopmental cohorts (PMID 40393460), supporting an anthropometric effect. BMI/obesity is a well-recognized, strongly correlated determinant of hip circumference, so under the stated rules this is best classified as "Existing," with some weight for "Established" given replication across independent cohorts. Other listed papers concern epilepsy, Parkinsonism, endometriosis, or the unrelated "BSN" acronym (bulbo-spinal neuronopathy) and are not relevant.

No articles were supplied for review, so there is no citable evidence linking FAM117A variants to mean corpuscular volume. Without at least one human genetic study reporting variants in this gene associated with MCV or a recognized precursor trait, the criteria for "Established" or "Existing" cannot be met. Likewise, no functional, expression, pathway, or animal-model data were provided to support a biologically "Hypothesized" relationship. The default classification on this empty evidence base is therefore "Novel," with small residual probability allocated to the other categories to account for literature that may exist but was not presented (e.g., large blood-cell-trait GWAS).

phenotype: Specific developmental disorders of scholastic skills
justification: ANKRD11 is unambiguously established as the cause of KBG syndrome through intragenic point/frameshift/missense variants in independent probands and families (PMID 21782149, 35833929, 27900361, 33955014), and the phenotype consistently includes developmental delay, intellectual disability and explicitly "learning disability" in milder/familial cases (PMID 22307766, 30877071). However, the queried phenotype, "specific developmental disorders of scholastic skills" (F81-type specific learning disorders), is not the primary reported outcome in these studies; the reported impairment is global (intellectual disability/global developmental delay) rather than circumscribed scholastic skill deficits. Cognitive profiling work in KBG (PMID 33917340) does show an uneven profile with relative weakness in perceptual reasoning, working memory and processing speed, which is a recognized substrate for scholastic skill difficulties, supporting at least an "Existing" relationship. Because the human variant evidence maps to a closely related but broader neurodevelopmental phenotype, I weight Existing slightly above Established, with little support for purely hypothesized or novel status.

The MARCHF8/MARCH8 articles exclusively concern E3 ubiquitin ligase biology in viral restriction (HIV-1, VSV-G, SARS-CoV-2, RSV, IAV, SADS-CoV), hepatocellular carcinoma, liver fibrosis, kidney injury, and IL-7R regulation, with no measurement of erythrocyte indices. The papers mentioning red cell distribution width are blood-donor microRNA studies (miR-142, miR-144, miR-451, miR-130a) that do not involve MARCHF8. The transplant phenomapping paper (PMID 29802085) co-mentions MARCH8 only as an AlloMap expression biomarker, unrelated to RDW. No human genetic variant association, no erythropoiesis-related mechanism, and no animal model linking MARCHF8 to RDW is presented, so the co-mentions are incidental.

phenotype: Erythrocytes [#/volume] in Blood by Automated count
justification: None of the provided articles report a quantitative genetic association (e.g., GWAS or cohort analysis) between PARN variants and automated erythrocyte count. However, multiple human reports describe germline PARN mutations causing dyskeratosis congenita/Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome and telomere biology disorders with bone marrow failure, cytopenias, and anemia (PMIDs 26810774, 33244623, 33035329, 25893598), which are well-recognized mechanisms directly affecting red cell numbers. Functional work shows PARN is required for TERC 3'-end maturation and that PAPD5 inhibition restores hematopoietic potential in telomere-disorder models (PMIDs 26482878, 30728146, 30930056), supporting biological plausibility but not variant-level association with the specific trait. Because the human evidence links PARN variants to bone marrow failure/cytopenias rather than to measured erythrocyte counts per se, "Existing" is the best fit, with residual weight on "Hypothesized."

Human germline hemizygous DOCK11 variants are reported in multiple independent families with immune dysregulation, autoimmune cytopenias (including thrombocytopenia) and, importantly, abnormal platelet ultrastructural morphology and spreading with impaired CDC42 activity (PMID 36952639), plus erythrocyte morphologic abnormalities (PMID 37342957). These are human genetic findings in platelet biology closely related to platelet size/morphology, supporting at least "Existing" status, but none of the listed articles directly measures or reports association with mean platelet volume as a quantitative trait, nor is a GWAS/cohort MPV association replicated here. Thus "Established" cannot be supported since no two papers report MPV-specific associations from their own results. Mechanistic support (DOCK11–CDC42–actin cytoskeleton regulation, essential for proplatelet formation and platelet size) also keeps substantial weight on "Hypothesized". "Novel" is unlikely given the demonstrated platelet structural phenotype in patients.

None of the supplied abstracts report an association between GIGYF1 variants and alkaline phosphatase levels. The strongest human genetic evidence concerns GIGYF1 predicted loss-of-function variants and glycemic traits (glucose, HbA1c, type 2 diabetes), cholesterol, IGF-1, hypothyroidism, obesity/BMI, clonal mosaicism, and cognitive function (PMIDs 34732801, 34234147, 35177841, 37072623, 41168175, 37231097), with only vague references to "blood biomarkers" in phenome-wide analyses (PMID 39842675) that do not specify alkaline phosphatase. A weak indirect rationale exists because GIGYF1 LoF carriers show broad adverse cardiometabolic/hepatic-adjacent biochemistry (lipids, IGF-1 signaling), which could plausibly extend to liver enzyme biomarkers, supporting some probability for Hypothesized. Mechanistic work (GRB10/IGF-1R signaling, autophagy in Drosophila, miRNA repression in C. elegans) is not ALP-specific and is largely non-human. Overall the gene–phenotype pair appears essentially unaddressed in this literature set, favoring Novel with residual weight on Hypothesized/Existing.

The strongest direct human evidence is the large exome/genome sequencing meta-analysis (PMID 40050430), which identified a novel rare coding variant burden association between MYBPC3 and atrial fibrillation in 52,416 cases, with broad replication in MyCode, deCODE and UK Biobank. Supporting human data come from a young-onset AF cohort in which MYBPC3 pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants were identified among probands (PMID 42619471) and from biobank analyses showing carriers of cardiomyopathy-predisposing variants (including MYBPC3) have markedly increased incident AF (PMID 35544052). Additionally, MYBPC3 is the most common cause of HCM, a well-recognized substrate/risk factor for AF, with MYBPC3-HCM cohorts showing high AF prevalence and fibrotic atrial substrate (PMIDs 41407035, 38819352, 26869393, 37271167). However, several HCM genotype-phenotype studies found MYH7 rather than MYBPC3 to carry the greater AF risk, and most MYBPC3 proband-level data describe AF as a secondary complication of cardiomyopathy rather than proving a direct monogenic cause of isolated AF, so points are split nearly evenly between Established and Existing.

All retrieved articles concern MTM1 variants causing X-linked myotubular/centronuclear myopathy; none report serum or plasma creatinine measurements, quantitative biochemical traits, or GWAS/association data for creatinine levels. There is therefore no human genetic evidence linking MTM1 variation to circulating creatinine, precluding "Established" or "Existing." A biologically plausible indirect link exists, since serum creatinine is strongly determined by skeletal muscle mass and MTM1 loss causes profound myofiber hypotrophy and muscle wasting, and one report notes multi-organ (hepatobiliary) involvement in XLMTM, which supports at most a hypothesized relationship. Because this reasoning is inferential rather than demonstrated in the cited literature, the weight falls mainly on Novel with a substantial share to Hypothesized.

Multiple independent human cohorts report associations between PLIN4 variants and weight/obesity phenotypes: PLIN4 11482G>A (rs894160) was associated with BMI in middle-aged Japanese males (PMID 20495294), with lower body weight/BMI and reduced obesity risk in Spanish White women (PMID 15355432), with body-weight regulation and fat loss during a VLCD/weight-maintenance trial (PMID 19385027), and with metabolic syndrome risk in obese children (PMID 18812483). Additionally, meta-analysis of rs8887 showed association with anthropometric traits plus a functional miR-522 mechanism (PMID 21533135), and large-scale UK Biobank exome analysis found rare loss-of-function PLIN4 variants adversely affect BMI-adjusted waist-to-hip ratio and fat distribution (PMID 34875679). Lifestyle-intervention weight-loss studies in Chinese Han adults (PMID 26725391) and GC/GNN supplementation (PMID 29361938) further support gene–environment modulation of weight. These are human genetic studies in independent populations, satisfying replication; mouse Plin4 knockout data (PMID 23423172) provide supportive but secondary biological evidence.

Multiple independent human GWAS report association of the BAK1/ZBTB9-BAK1 locus with platelet count: a Korean GWAS of 8,842 discovery plus 7,861 replication subjects found 6p21 BAK1 variants (PMID 25705162), a Hispanic/Latino GWAS of 12,491 participants discovered and replicated the ZBTB9-BAK1 locus (PMID 26805783), and a Dutch cohort with British twin replication confirmed BAK1 among known platelet count loci (PMID 29066854). Further human genetic support comes from rs5745568 in BAK1, a platelet-count-lowering allele, associating with dengue hemorrhagic fever in 918 Thai patients (PMID 27401010), and from platelet-count SNPs near BAK1 linked to ALL risk (PMIDs 32467347, 31767839). Biological plausibility is strong, since BAK1 is a pro-apoptotic effector governing platelet lifespan and Bak-deficient mice show elevated platelet counts (PMID 24464220), supporting the genetic findings mechanistically. Because at least two independent human cohorts report the association in their own results, the Established category is best supported, with a small residual allocation to Existing given that one signal is intergenic (ZBTB9-BAK1).

No article reports human genetic variants in CCNA2 associated with body weight or related anthropometric traits; the human studies here concern cancer prognosis, tumor expression, and protein biochemistry, where weight is not examined. Weight appears only as an incidental measurement in animal studies (mice, goats, dairy cows) in which CCNA2 is one of many cell-cycle transcripts altered alongside growth, liver/body weight ratios, or mammary/muscle development (PMIDs 38929389, 38085574, 38023376, 34304871, 25682855, 38144278, 42675227). These provide, at most, weak indirect biological plausibility via proliferation and tissue growth, which supports "Hypothesized" rather than "Existing," since no human variant evidence exists. A substantial probability remains for "Novel," because most co-mentions of weight are purely incidental descriptors of experimental animals rather than evidence that CCNA2 activity influences body weight.

None of the listed articles reports red cell distribution width (RDW) as a measured outcome, and no GWAS or association study of LCAT variants with RDW is present, so "Established" cannot be supported (no two independent human studies with variants tied to RDW). However, multiple human reports of LCAT loss-of-function mutations in families and probands describe normochromic/hemolytic anemia and abnormal erythrocyte membrane lipid composition with altered red cell morphology (target cells, anisocytosis-related changes), phenotypes mechanistically and clinically linked to increased RDW (PMIDs 11957819, 24174160, 32618730, 3141686, 806250, 4640953). Proteomic work in human LCAT-deficiency carriers also shows haptoglobin reduction consistent with chronic hemolysis (PMID 30529744). This supports "Existing" (human variants associated with a strongly linked precursor/mechanism phenotype), with residual weight on "Hypothesized" since the RDW parameter itself is never assessed and some supporting evidence is biochemical/animal-based.

Every provided article concerns SPTB (erythroid β-spectrin) in red blood cell membrane disorders — hereditary spherocytosis, elliptocytosis, and pyropoikilocytosis — with phenotypes of hemolytic anemia, jaundice, reticulocytosis, and splenectomy; none report platelet counts, mean platelet volume, platelet function, or thrombocytopenia. No human study here demonstrates variants in SPTB associated with a platelet trait, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported by this evidence base. A modest Hypothesized weight is justified because spectrin-based membrane skeletons are generically relevant to blood cell (including platelet) membrane mechanics, and splenectomy in HS patients secondarily alters platelet counts, but these are indirect and not gene-variant-to-platelet evidence. The SPTBN1 paper (PMID 33847457) is about a neurodevelopmental phenotype and a different gene, further weakening any platelet link.

No article in this set reports a genetic association between RB1CC1 and hip circumference itself. The closest human genetic evidence is a large exome-wide rare-variant study in 340,319 UK Biobank participants where RB1CC1 was an exome-wide significant gene for hand grip strength (PMID 37301943), a body-composition/muscle-mass-related trait, and a single de novo RB1CC1 duplication case presenting with schizophrenia and obesity (PMID 33340270), which is only a single proband with a CNV and therefore insufficient for Established. Supporting biology is strong but mechanistic rather than phenotype-specific: RB1CC1/FIP200 regulates TSC1–TSC2 and mTORC1 signaling and determines cell size in muscle and neurons (PMIDs 16865226, 16043512, 19211835), which plausibly links it to body size and adiposity traits. Most remaining papers are autophagy reviews or schizophrenia rare-variant studies that co-mention RB1CC1 without relevance to anthropometry. Hence weight falls mainly on Hypothesized, with meaningful probability for Existing via the muscle-strength and obesity findings and some residual for Novel.
